claim: Logging a lesson you give: what 61.51(h)(2) requires
old: endorse the student's logbook with a description of the training, its length, your signature and your certificate number (61.51(h)(2)).
new: endorse the student's logbook legibly with a description of the training, the length of the lesson, your signature, your certificate number, and "certificate expiration date or recent experience end date" (61.51(h)(2)). A commercial pilot certificate has no expiration date (61.19(c)).
source: 14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)(i)-(ii): 'Be endorsed in a legible manner by the authorized instructor; and Include a description of the training given, the length of the training lesson, and the authorized instructor's signature, certificate number, and certificate expiration date or recent experience end date, consistent with the requirements of § 61.197.' 14 CFR 61.19(c)(1): a pilot certificate is issued without an expiration date. eCFR as of 2026-10-19. Brian's 'instructor's practice' line left unchanged.

'about 120 ft per °C' density-altitude step (open item)
old: The 120 ft per °C step is an approximation.
new: The 120 ft per °C step is a common rule of thumb, an approximation.
source: No FAA source found that states it. Searched FAA-H-8083-25C, FAA-H-8083-28B (incl. Appendix C, which uses a chart only), FAA-H-8083-11B, and FAA-P-8740-02 'Density Altitude' (faasafety.gov copy). P-8740-02's 'Density Altitude Rule-of-Thumb Chart' is in °F and implies roughly 103-115 ft per °C, so 120 slightly overstates it. Kept labelled as a rule of thumb; the card's own AWH comparison (13,000 vs 12,700 ft) shows the size of the error. No citation added.
